newsitem.title: MEXICO: Controversial Mexican group gets election funding.
newsitem.headline: Controversial Mexican group gets election funding.

text.p: A Mexican human rights group has finally been given the go-ahead to launch a controversial project to monitor campaign spending just three weeks before mid-term elections next month.

In March, the Mexican government blocked some $400,000 of European Union funding for the Mexican Human Rights Academy. The money was to have financed one of the first-ever studies of campaign spending in Mexico's tainted electoral history.

The Academy's Oscar Ortiz, in charge of the monitoring project, told Reuters it received some 510,000 pesos ($65,000) last week via the United Nations Development Programme to get underway. But the delay had badly crimped it.

"There's enormous time pressure, we 're already practically on the eve of the elections," Ortiz said. The elections for the lower house in Congress, a quarter of the senate and the mayor of Mexico City are to be held on July 6.
"We had planned to start working last November. Starting 20 or 25 days before the elections means we have to make a very serious adjustment in the quality (of the project)," he added.

Mexico's Foreign Ministry caused an uproar in March when it blocked European Union funding for the Academy, saying it violated the terms of a cooperation agreement between the two sides. It refused to back down despite criticism from top electoral officials.

Ortiz said his scaled-back project would analyse campaigning in the streets and underground rail system of Mexico City, campaign meetings and media exposure over a two-week period starting last Saturday.

Mexico's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), which has ruled for 68 years, has often been accused of exceeding spending limits during campaigns. In the Mexico City elections, polls show its candidate running a distant second or even third to leftist Cuauhtemoc Cardenas of the Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).
